title: What Makes a Li‑Ion Cell Tick?

segments.text: Ever wonder what makes a Li‑ion cell tick?
Energy lives in reversible intercalation of Li⁺ into solid electrodes.
The negative electrode is usually graphite, sometimes blended with silicon to add capacity.
The positive electrode may be LiCoO₂, LiFePO₄, a nickel‑manganese‑cobalt mix, or NCA alloy.
Between them the electrolyte—lithium hexafluorophosphate in organic carbonates—conducts lithium ions but does not react chemically.
Ions slip through the liquid while electrons travel the external circuit, delivering power to your device.
That whole process is what makes a cell exactly tick.

question: Which part of the cell moves ions while electrons travel the circuit?
